Build for the Model You Will Have in Six Months

The capability curve is steep enough now that the model you are optimizing around today will be obsolete before your project ships. The teams that win build thin, swappable, eval-anchored systems, so every model upgrade is a one-day win instead of a rebuild.

Here is the pattern I keep running into on client work. A team spends three months building an elaborate scaffolding around a model: a careful prompt-decomposition chain, a retry-and-repair loop to catch the model's mistakes, a 600-line system prompt that encodes every edge case they hit. It works. They are proud of it. Then a new model lands, and most of that scaffolding is now dead weight, because the new model does in one step what they built forty steps to compensate for.

They optimized around the model in front of them. That is the most expensive mistake in applied AI right now, and almost everyone makes it.

Three things to take away:

  • Model capability is moving on an exponential. Most organizations are absorbing it on a linear. The gap between what AI can do and what your company actually does with it is widening, and it is not a model problem. It is an architecture and a discipline problem.
  • The teams that pull ahead do not build clever workarounds for today's model's weaknesses. They build thin systems on simple primitives, keep a shelf of evals that almost pass, and make swapping in a new model a half-day task instead of a quarter.
  • The shift to internalize is from asking a model to do a task to asking it to own an outcome. That requires you to define what good looks like up front, which is the one piece of work that does not get automated away.

The gap is not where you think it is

Model intelligence is improving faster than at any point I have worked through, and the intervals between jumps keep shrinking. A couple of years ago the frontier was drafting a usable commit message. Then it was building a whole feature unattended. Then it was running overnight on a long task and staying coherent. Now models read an entire codebase, find a defect that slipped past human review for years, and propose the fix.

Business capability is not moving on that curve. Most organizations are improving in straight lines: a bit more automation this quarter, a slightly faster process next quarter. So the distance between what the model can do and what the company has wired it to do gets bigger every few months, not smaller.

That gap is the whole opportunity, and the reason it stays open is rarely the model. It is that the systems around the model were built for a version that no longer exists, and they cannot absorb the new one without a rebuild. You do not close the gap by waiting for a smarter model. You close it by building so the next model lands cleanly.

Stop architecting around today's weaknesses

Most AI scaffolding exists to paper over a specific weakness of a specific model. The model hallucinates a field, so you add a validator. It loses the thread on long inputs, so you chunk and orchestrate. It cannot follow a multi-part instruction, so you decompose the instruction into a chain of smaller calls.

Every one of those is a reasonable response to a real limitation. Every one of them also becomes a liability the moment the limitation goes away. The decomposition chain that rescued you on last year's model now gets in the way of a model that would have handled the whole thing in one pass, and handled it better than your hand-tuned steps do.

The counterintuitive lesson, and the one I push hardest with engineering teams, is that as the model gets more capable, your scaffolding should get thinner, not thicker. A more intelligent model goes farther with basic primitives, a real filesystem, a sandbox it can run code in, the ability to execute its own tests, a few sharp tools, and it goes less far when it is trapped inside an elaborate harness that was designed to compensate for things it no longer struggles with.

When you find yourself adding another layer of control, ask whether you are solving a durable problem or a temporary one. If it is temporary, you are building something you will have to tear out.

Keep a shelf of things that almost work

The hardest part of moving on an exponential is that you cannot feel it day to day. The model gets better underneath you and nothing in your product tells you. So you keep shipping for the capability you had when you started.

The practical fix is a discipline, not a tool. Keep a shelf of eval prototypes for the things that are just out of reach today. Every time you try something and the current model cannot quite do it, do not throw the attempt away. Write it down as a small, repeatable test, tag it as "not yet," and keep it. A messy multi-step workflow that falls apart halfway. A judgment call the model gets wrong more often than right. A design task that comes out almost good enough.

Then run that shelf against every new model. Most of the time nothing changes. But every so often one of those "not yet" prototypes flips and starts passing. That is not a curiosity. That is the single clearest signal you will ever get that the ground moved, and it is your cue to ship something you could not have shipped a month ago.

This is how you turn an invisible exponential into a visible event. Without the shelf, you find out the model got better when a competitor ships the thing you also could have built. With the shelf, you find out the morning the eval goes green.

Make model upgrades boring

If swapping in a new model means a month of re-validation, you will not do it often, and you will fall behind teams that do. The goal is to make a model upgrade a half-day regression test, not a quarter-long migration.

That means automated evals that actually represent your real work, run on every candidate model, with a pass or fail you trust. It means keeping the model choice loose enough in your architecture that changing it is a config line, not a refactor. It means staying hands-on with each new release the week it lands, pushing your own hard cases through it rather than reading someone else's benchmark.

The teams I see winning treat every model upgrade as a business opportunity instead of a maintenance cost. A new release is not a thing that might break their pipeline. It is a chance to retire a workaround, raise a quality bar, or open a use case that was not viable last month. The difference between those two postures is almost entirely whether they built to upgrade easily in the first place.

From doing tasks to owning outcomes

There is a shift in how you use a capable model that changes what you can ask for. The useful frame is time horizon, how long a model can work on its own before it loses the thread of what it is doing. As that horizon stretches from minutes to hours to days, the unit of work you hand over changes.

You stop asking for tasks and start handing over outcomes. Instead of asking a model to write this week's project update, you give it responsibility for keeping the project on track and surfacing what needs attention. Instead of asking for a financial forecast, you tell it to own the forecast, update it as new numbers land, and keep it accurate. The model is no longer producing an artifact on request. It is holding a goal over time.

That only works if you do one thing well, and it is the thing that does not get automated. You have to define what good looks like, clearly enough that the work can be checked against it. A rubric. A spec. A condition a machine can verify. I call this setting the bar, and it is the front half of the only two jobs that stay human as the agents take the middle: you set the bar before the work, and you hold the bar after it. The agent crosses the distance between. Hand a capable model a vague intent and you get confident, useless output. Hand it a clear bar and the autonomy finally pays off.

The gap closes on your side, not theirs

The frontier labs will keep doing their part. The model will keep getting smarter, and faster, and the intervals will keep shrinking. None of that closes the gap between what AI can do and what your organization actually does with it. That gap closes on your side of the line.

It closes when your systems are thin enough to let a better model show what it can do. It closes when you have a shelf of evals ready to tell you the moment something new becomes possible. It closes when an upgrade is a Tuesday, not a project. Build for the model you will have in six months, because at this pace, you will have it, and the only question is whether you are ready to use it the day it arrives.
